questions.stem: A patient is brought to hospital with severe dehydration. Their blood tests show increased blood solute concentration and decreased blood volume. Which homeostatic mechanism would their body activate first?

options.text: Increased sweating to cool the body down
Increased ADH release to retain more water in the kidneys
Decreased heart rate to conserve energy
Increased urine production to flush out excess solutes

questions.explanation: When blood is too concentrated (dehydrated), osmoreceptors in the hypothalamus detect this and stimulate the pituitary gland to release more ADH. ADH acts on the kidneys to reabsorb more water, helping to restore blood concentration to normal — a classic example of homeostasis.

questions.stem: A student defines homeostasis as 'keeping everything in the body the same.' Why is this definition not quite accurate?

options.text: Because homeostasis only applies to temperature regulation
Because homeostasis maintains a relatively stable internal environment, with conditions fluctuating around set points rather than being perfectly constant
Because homeostasis means the body never changes at all
Because homeostasis only occurs during sleep

questions.explanation: Homeostasis is the regulation of internal conditions to maintain a relatively stable environment, despite external changes. Conditions like temperature and blood glucose do fluctuate, but negative feedback mechanisms bring them back towards optimal set points — they are not kept perfectly constant.

questions.stem: In a negative feedback loop for body temperature, the sequence is: stimulus → receptor → coordination centre → effector → response. If body temperature rises above 37°C, which component detects this change?

options.text: Sweat glands (effectors)
The hypothalamus acting as both receptor and coordination centre
The skin surface
The muscles (effectors)

questions.explanation: The hypothalamus in the brain contains thermoreceptors that detect changes in blood temperature. It also acts as the coordination centre, sending nerve impulses to effectors (like sweat glands and blood vessels) to bring temperature back to the set point.

questions.stem: Why is it important that enzymes in the human body operate within a narrow temperature range maintained by homeostasis?

options.text: Enzymes work equally well at all temperatures
Enzymes have an optimum temperature; too far above this and they denature, losing their function
Enzymes are only needed during exercise when body temperature changes
Enzymes produce heat, so temperature regulation prevents overheating

questions.explanation: Enzymes are proteins with specific 3D shapes. They work best at their optimum temperature (around 37°C for human enzymes). If temperature rises too high, the enzyme denatures — its active site changes shape and it can no longer catalyse reactions. Homeostasis keeps temperature within the range enzymes need.

questions.stem: A thermostat in a house turns the heating on when the temperature drops below 20°C and off when it exceeds 20°C. This is often used as an analogy for biological homeostasis. What type of feedback does this represent?

options.text: Positive feedback — the response amplifies the original change
Negative feedback — the response counteracts the original change to restore the set point
No feedback — the thermostat operates independently
Positive feedback — the heating stays on indefinitely

questions.explanation: This is negative feedback: when temperature drops (the change), the heating turns on (the response) to raise the temperature back up, counteracting the original change. When the set point is reached, the heating turns off. Most homeostatic mechanisms in the body use negative feedback.
